title: Super Tuscans
subtitle: Breaking the rules
objectives: Explain how the Super Tuscans began
Explain their effect on Italian law

steps.title: The rebels
steps.body: In the 1960s and 1970s, Chianti rules required white grapes in the blend and limited international grapes. Some producers wanted to make the best wine they could instead. Sassicaia, first sold in 1971, used Cabernet Sauvignon. Tignanello, in 1971, blended Sangiovese with Cabernet in small barrels, with no white grapes.

steps.title: Table wine prices
steps.body: Because they broke DOC rules, these wines had to be sold as Vino da Tavola, the lowest category, yet sold for more than any Chianti. The press named them Super Tuscans. In 1992, Italy created IGT to give them a category; Sassicaia got its own DOC in 2013. Chianti Classico's rules changed too.

steps.prompt: The first Super Tuscans had to be labelled as simple table wine.
steps.explanation: Yes. Breaking DOC rules meant they could only be sold as Vino da Tavola.

steps.title: Today
steps.body: Super Tuscans include Sangiovese-based wines, like Flaccianello and Pergole Torte, which is pure Sangiovese, and Bordeaux blends from Bolgheri, like Ornellaia. Many use small French oak. Since Chianti Classico now allows 100% Sangiovese, some producers have returned to the DOCG.

steps.explanation: Barolo is a Piedmont DOCG made from Nebbiolo.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Super Tuscans broke DOC rules in the 1970s
They led to the IGT category in 1992
They include Sangiovese and Bordeaux-style wines
